FINAL EXPERIMENT DESIGN (design only — no execution, no results claimed)

Title: Ablation study of dynamic memory lookup and unit representations in InfLLM

=====================================================================
1. RATIONALE
=====================================================================
Question decomposed: "How critical are X (dynamic context memory lookup) and Y (choice of unit representations) to InfLLM's performance?" Criticality is operationalized as the performance drop each component's degradation causes, and whether the two components interact.

Mapping of the assumed InfLLM mechanism to the two factors:
- Factor A targets the *selection policy*: which memory blocks a query token attends to. InfLLM (as assumed) computes, per query token, a key and scores it against block keys, selecting top-k blocks, plus an always-on local sliding window. Removing or degrading this policy changes the information routing without changing what is stored.
- Factor B targets the *content of the routing signal*: how each block is compressed into a unit representation (assumed: a block reader using a representative token plus learnable gating). Changing this changes the fidelity of the key/value signal used for both selection (via block keys) and reading (via block contents). B alone changes representation; A alone changes selection; A×B captures whether a good representation is only useful when selection is query-conditioned (the hypothesized interaction).

Independent vs. joint contributions: a 4×4 factorial (4 levels of A × 4 levels of B) lets us estimate (i) main effect of lookup policy, (ii) main effect of representation scheme, and (iii) the A×B interaction — e.g., whether mean-pooled keys are nearly as good as block-reader keys under full top-k selection but collapse under k=1, which would indicate the representation's criticality is contingent on lookup precision.

EXPLICIT ASSUMPTIONS ABOUT INFLLM (unverified; to be confirmed from the paper/reference implementation before any run):
(A1) Base model: Llama-2-7B with InfLLM's trained adaptation parameters. Unverified — scale and base checkpoint are assumptions.
(A2) Mechanism: context split into fixed-size memory blocks (block size assumed in the thousands of tokens; exact value unverified); per-block unit representation computed by a block reader using a representative token + learnable gating; query-conditioned top-k selection (k small, exact value unverified) over block keys; local sliding window always active.
(A3) Training-free inference: block-selection machinery is learned on short sequences (~8k tokens, assumed) and applied zero-shot to long contexts; therefore factor manipulations are implementable at inference time without retraining.
(A4) Tasks: long-context LM perplexity and retrieval/QA suites are the standard evaluation surface.
Any mismatch between these assumptions and the actual implementation (e.g., learned top-k thresholds, different block-reader construction) requires arm redefinition but not redesign of the factorial structure.

=====================================================================
2. FULL ARM SPECIFICATION
=====================================================================
Factor A — dynamic memory lookup policy (4 levels):
- A1 (reference): Full InfLLM. Query-conditioned top-k selection over block keys + local sliding window. Everything as assumed from the paper.
- A2 (removal / dense): No dynamic lookup. Attention over ALL blocks uniformly — i.e., naive long-context attention restricted to the same block partition, same local window. This isolates the value of selective routing given the same stored memory.
- A3 (static/position-based, budget-matched): Select the same number of blocks as A1 (top-k), but by position (blocks nearest the query) or by a fixed, query-independent pattern. Same compute and same number of attended blocks as A1 — this is the key OOD-confound control (see §3).
- A4 (random, budget-matched): Select k blocks uniformly at random per query token (fixed seed per example). Same budget as A1, selection signal destroyed.
- A5 (budget sweep, optional secondary): top-k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} with A1's policy, to map the sensitivity curve of selection precision. Analyzed as a dose-response sub-study, not part of the 4×4 core.

Factor B — unit representation scheme (4 levels):
- B1 (reference): Original block-reader unit representations (representative token + learnable gating), as assumed.
- B2: Mean-pooled block encodings — mean over block token hidden states, projected to the key space.
- B3: Single-token keys — the block's representative token's hidden state only, no gating.
- B4 (floor control): Degenerate keys — frozen random projections of block content (or even fixed random vectors per block index), refreshed per seed. Establishes the selection-signal floor: performance when block keys carry no task-relevant signal.

Nuisance scale-matching (critical for clean B attribution): substituting keys changes their norm/scale, which after softmax temperature acts as an effective temperature change, not just a signal change. For B2–B4, normalize replacement keys to match the L2 norm distribution of B1 keys (per-layer, per-head if applicable), and verify empirically that the top-k selection entropy distribution over blocks is comparable for B1 vs. B2 on a calibration subset before the main run. Additionally: value/pathway (what is actually attended to after selection) is held IDENTICAL across B arms — only the routing key changes — so B isolates the representation's role in routing, not in reading. (If the assumed block reader also affects the read-out pathway, add a B1-read/B2-route cross arm to decompose this; treat as a design contingency.)

Core factorial: A1–A4 × B1–B4 (16 arms) + A5 sweep (5 extra runs at B1, optionally one at B2). All arms share identical block partitioning, block size, local window size, KV storage, sampling/decoding settings.

=====================================================================
3. CONTROLS
=====================================================================
- Sliding-window-only baseline: local window active, memory machinery disabled entirely. Establishes what the memory adds at all.
- Short-context reference: base model (or InfLLM within its trained context length, assumed 8k) evaluated on truncated versions of the same inputs — separates "long-context ability" from "short-context competence."
- Fixed geometry: block size, number of stored blocks, local window, and total attention budget held constant across all arms so effects are attributable to policy/representation, not to compute or coverage.
- OOD-regime confound control: A2 (uniform attention over all blocks) both removes selection AND changes the attention distribution regime. A3 and A4 keep the regime (same sparse top-k structure, same budget) and change only the selection signal; the contrast A1 − A3/A4 measures the value of *informed* selection, while A1 − A2 additionally includes any regime shift. If A2 performs similarly to A3/A4, the regime confound is negligible; if A2 performs markedly differently, interpret its effect as "selection + regime" jointly and rely on A3/A4 for the pure selection effect.
- Seeds: ≥3 seeds per arm where stochasticity exists (A4 explicitly seeded; decoding greedy/deterministic for generation tasks). Report seed-level variance; for deterministic arms, replicate over dataset subsamples.
- Order/position sanity check: verify block scores vary with query position across contexts in A1 (a positive control that selection is actually dynamic and non-degenerate before ablations).
- Calibration gate (from §2): key-scale matching verified on a held-out calibration slice; if B2/B4 entropy distributions are wildly different, re-tune normalization before main runs.

=====================================================================
4. ANALYSIS PLAN
=====================================================================
Metrics per suite:
- Long-context LM: per-token perplexity / NLL as a function of context length (bucketed, e.g., 4k–64k+), plus local vs. distant token NLL splits (distant-token NLL is the most sensitive to memory behavior; local should be nearly flat across arms — an internal sanity check).
- Needle-in-a-haystack: exact retrieval accuracy by depth × context-length grid.
- QA/summarization (LongBench/ZeroSCROLLS-style): task metric (F1/EM/ROUGE), with input-length stratification.

Statistical analysis:
- Two-way factorial ANOVA-style decomposition (or mixed-effects model with seed/dataset random effects) on each metric: main effect of A, main effect of B, A×B interaction, with bootstrap CIs (cluster bootstrap over documents).
- Effect sizes reported as absolute deltas vs. A1×B1 and as Cohen's d-style standardized effects; paired comparisons (same inputs across arms) to maximize power.
- Interaction interpretation: e.g., if B2 ≈ B1 under A1 but B2 ≪ B1 under A4/A3, representation quality matters only when selection is dynamic — the joint-contribution answer. If main effect of A is large and B effects are flat, lookup is critical and representation is redundant; if B4 (random keys) ≈ B1, the selection signal itself is not doing the work (suspicious — triggers a mechanism audit); if A3/A4 ≈ A1, "dynamic" lookup per se adds nothing beyond budget-matched static selection.
- Decision criteria (pre-registered thresholds, to be finalized once baseline variance is known): a component is "critical" if its ablation costs >10% relative on retrieval accuracy or >0.2 nats/token on distant-token NLL with CIs excluding zero, across ≥2 task suites; "redundant" if deltas are within noise (<2% / <0.05 nats); intermediate results reported as graded sensitivity rather than forced into binary labels. The A×B interaction is deemed meaningful only if its effect size exceeds the sum of marginal main-effect predictions with CI excluding zero.
- A5 sweep analyzed as monotonic sensitivity of performance to k; the k at which performance saturates indicates how much selection precision is needed.

=====================================================================
5. FEASIBILITY AND RISKS
=====================================================================
- Primary design is inference-only: justified because (per assumption A3) InfLLM is trained for short contexts and applied training-free to long ones, so ablations of the selection policy and key construction are implementable by modifying inference code, not weights. Cost: 16 core arms + 5 sweep runs + 2 controls ≈ 23 configurations; at 7B, 32k-token contexts, a few hundred to a few thousand examples per suite — nontrivial but tractable on a single A100-class GPU over days. If any ablation requires retraining (e.g., if the block reader is entangled with read-out in the actual implementation), cost grows by orders of magnitude; the trained-variant path (re-fitting adaptation parameters per arm on the assumed 8k training recipe) is listed as an extension, not the primary design.
- Scale assumptions: 7B primary. A small proxy (e.g., 1B-class model with the same mechanism re-implemented) may be used for smoke tests only (verifying arm implementations, calibration gates); it is explicitly NOT conclusion-supporting, because block-selection behavior may not transfer across scales.
- Benchmark availability offline: datasets (PG19/proof-pile subsets, NIAH generators, LongBench/ZeroSCROLLS) are not present in the sandbox and network is disabled; obtainability in the execution environment is unconfirmed and is a gating feasibility item.
- Compute/runtime budget is an unknown: no GPU here, no dependency environment; the numbers above are planning estimates, not verified runtimes.
- Main risks: (i) architecture assumptions wrong → arms redefined (factorial structure survives); (ii) OOD confound on A2 → mitigated by budget-matched A3/A4; (iii) key-scale nuisance in B → mitigated by normalization + entropy calibration gate; (iv) B4 floor control may be too degenerate (uniform selection) making it partially an A-arm — mitigated by seeding random keys with content-correlated noise (random projection retains some signal) and interpreting B4 as a floor, not a pure B level; (v) interaction effects may be small relative to seed/document variance → paired designs and clustering over documents.

=====================================================================
6. SCOPE STATEMENT
=====================================================================
This is a design-only deliverable. No experiment has been run, no data collected, and no results are claimed. The expected empirical outcome — which of dynamic lookup and unit representations is critical, redundant, or interacting — is unknown a priori; the design is built to distinguish these outcomes rather than anticipate them. All InfLLM-specific details (base model, scale, block size, top-k, block-reader construction, training recipe) are assumptions from background knowledge, flagged above, and must be verified against the paper and reference implementation before execution.

Here's what I found, followed by the proposed high-level approach.

## 1. What is actually present

**Repository contents (`/workspace`):**
- Only a single file: `task.json`, which contains the question itself plus a documents map saying `track.md: "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required."` There is no actual `track.md` file, no InfLLM source code, no papers, no datasets, and no model checkpoints anywhere in the sandbox.
- Environment: network disabled, no GPU, system Python only, no project dependencies preinstalled.

**Consequence for the architecture description:** I cannot point to any in-repository documentation of (a) the dynamic context memory / block-selection mechanism or (b) how memory units (block representations) are constructed. Everything below about InfLLM's architecture comes from my background knowledge of the InfLLM paper (training-free long-context extrapolation with a block-based context memory, built on Llama-2-7B: contexts split into memory blocks, each block summarized by a *block reader* into a unit representation/key using a representative token + learnable gating; at inference each query token selects top-k blocks via similarity between its key and block keys, combined with a sliding local-attention window). **These details are unverified against the supplied materials and must be treated as assumptions, not facts.** The researcher should confirm the exact mechanism (block size, top-k, block-reader construction) if source is available.

## 2. Proposed high-level experimental approach

A **factorial ablation design**, inference-only where possible, comparing arms against the full InfLLM configuration on standard long-context tasks:

**Factor A — dynamic memory lookup (degrade/remove):**
- A1: Full InfLLM (query-conditioned top-k block selection + local sliding window).
- A2: No dynamic lookup — attend uniformly over all blocks (i.e., naive long-context attention with the same block partition).
- A3: Static lookup — select blocks by position only (e.g., blocks near the query) or fixed/random selection, preserving the block machinery but removing query-conditioning.
- A4: Lookup-budget sensitivity — vary top-k (e.g., k=1, 2, 4, 8) to test how much retrieval precision matters.

**Factor B — unit representations (replace/degrade):**
- B1: Original block-reader unit representations (representative token + gating).
- B2: Mean-pooled block encodings.
- B3: Single-token keys (representative token only, no gating).
- B4: Degenerate keys (frozen random projections) — a floor control isolating whether selection signal matters.

**Controls:** sliding-window-only baseline (memory disabled); short-context model evaluated directly (zero-shot extrapolation baseline); identical block size, local window, and inference settings across arms.

**Task suites (all retrieval-style + LM):** long-context LM perplexity (e.g., PG19 / proof-pile subsets), needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, ZeroSCROLLS / LongBench-style QA and summarization. Metrics: perplexity, retrieval accuracy, ROUGE/F1/EM with seed-level CIs; analysis via two-way factorial effect estimates (Factor A × Factor B interaction) to answer whether the two components are independently or jointly critical.

## 3. Key assumptions and uncertainties

**Assumptions (stated, not verified):**
- InfLLM's mechanism matches my recollection above; ablations are implementable at inference time without retraining (training-free design supports this).
- A reference implementation could be obtained/ported; evaluation harness and datasets could be assembled.

**Uncertainties / flagged as unconfirmable from available materials:**
- No code, paper, or checkpoint exists in the sandbox; nothing confirms model scale (7B assumed per paper) or exact hyperparameters (block size, top-k, block-reader details).

Title: Ablation study of dynamic memory lookup and unit representations in InfLLM

=====================================================================
1. RATIONALE
=====================================================================
Question decomposed: "How critical are X (dynamic context memory lookup) and Y (choice of unit representations) to InfLLM's performance?" Criticality is operationalized as the performance drop each component's degradation causes, and whether the two components interact.

Mapping of the assumed InfLLM mechanism to the two factors:
- Factor A targets the *selection policy*: which memory blocks a query token attends to. InfLLM (as assumed) computes, per query token, a key and scores it against block keys, selecting top-k blocks, plus an always-on local sliding window. Removing or degrading this policy changes the information routing without changing what is stored.
- Factor B targets the *content of the routing signal*: how each block is compressed into a unit representation (assumed: a block reader using a representative token plus learnable gating). Changing this changes the fidelity of the key/value signal used for both selection (via block keys) and reading (via block contents). B alone changes representation; A alone changes selection; A×B captures whether a good representation is only useful when selection is query-conditioned (the hypothesized interaction).

Independent vs. joint contributions: a 4×4 factorial (4 levels of A × 4 levels of B) lets us estimate (i) main effect of lookup policy, (ii) main effect of representation scheme, and (iii) the A×B interaction — e.g., whether mean-pooled keys are nearly as good as block-reader keys under full top-k selection but collapse under k=1, which would indicate the representation's criticality is contingent on lookup precision.

EXPLICIT ASSUMPTIONS ABOUT INFLLM (unverified; to be confirmed from the paper/reference implementation before any run):
(A1) Base model: Llama-2-7B with InfLLM's trained adaptation parameters. Unverified — scale and base checkpoint are assumptions.
(A2) Mechanism: context split into fixed-size memory blocks (block size assumed in the thousands of tokens; exact value unverified); per-block unit representation computed by a block reader using a representative token + learnable gating; query-conditioned top-k selection (k small, exact value unverified) over block keys; local sliding window always active.
(A3) Training-free inference: block-selection machinery is learned on short sequences (~8k tokens, assumed) and applied zero-shot to long contexts; therefore factor manipulations are implementable at inference time without retraining.
(A4) Tasks: long-context LM perplexity and retrieval/QA suites are the standard evaluation surface.
Any mismatch between these assumptions and the actual implementation (e.g., learned top-k thresholds, different block-reader construction) requires arm redefinition but not redesign of the factorial structure.

=====================================================================
2. FULL ARM SPECIFICATION
=====================================================================
Factor A — dynamic memory lookup policy (4 levels):
- A1 (reference): Full InfLLM. Query-conditioned top-k selection over block keys + local sliding window. Everything as assumed from the paper.
- A2 (removal / dense): No dynamic lookup. Attention over ALL blocks uniformly — i.e., naive long-context attention restricted to the same block partition, same local window. This isolates the value of selective routing given the same stored memory.
- A3 (static/position-based, budget-matched): Select the same number of blocks as A1 (top-k), but by position (blocks nearest the query) or by a fixed, query-independent pattern. Same compute and same number of attended blocks as A1 — this is the key OOD-confound control (see §3).
- A4 (random, budget-matched): Select k blocks uniformly at random per query token (fixed seed per example). Same budget as A1, selection signal destroyed.
- A5 (budget sweep, optional secondary): top-k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} with A1's policy, to map the sensitivity curve of selection precision. Analyzed as a dose-response sub-study, not part of the 4×4 core.

Factor B — unit representation scheme (4 levels):
- B1 (reference): Original block-reader unit representations (representative token + learnable gating), as assumed.
- B2: Mean-pooled block encodings — mean over block token hidden states, projected to the key space.
- B3: Single-token keys — the block's representative token's hidden state only, no gating.
- B4 (floor control): Degenerate keys — frozen random projections of block content (or even fixed random vectors per block index), refreshed per seed. Establishes the selection-signal floor: performance when block keys carry no task-relevant signal.

Nuisance scale-matching (critical for clean B attribution): substituting keys changes their norm/scale, which after softmax temperature acts as an effective temperature change, not just a signal change. For B2–B4, normalize replacement keys to match the L2 norm distribution of B1 keys (per-layer, per-head if applicable), and verify empirically that the top-k selection entropy distribution over blocks is comparable for B1 vs. B2 on a calibration subset before the main run. Additionally: value/pathway (what is actually attended to after selection) is held IDENTICAL across B arms — only the routing key changes — so B isolates the representation's role in routing, not in reading. (If the assumed block reader also affects the read-out pathway, add a B1-read/B2-route cross arm to decompose this; treat as a design contingency.)

Core factorial: A1–A4 × B1–B4 (16 arms) + A5 sweep (5 extra runs at B1, optionally one at B2). All arms share identical block partitioning, block size, local window size, KV storage, sampling/decoding settings.

=====================================================================
3. CONTROLS
=====================================================================
- Sliding-window-only baseline: local window active, memory machinery disabled entirely. Establishes what the memory adds at all.
- Short-context reference: base model (or InfLLM within its trained context length, assumed 8k) evaluated on truncated versions of the same inputs — separates "long-context ability" from "short-context competence."
- Fixed geometry: block size, number of stored blocks, local window, and total attention budget held constant across all arms so effects are attributable to policy/representation, not to compute or coverage.
- OOD-regime confound control: A2 (uniform attention over all blocks) both removes selection AND changes the attention distribution regime. A3 and A4 keep the regime (same sparse top-k structure, same budget) and change only the selection signal; the contrast A1 − A3/A4 measures the value of *informed* selection, while A1 − A2 additionally includes any regime shift. If A2 performs similarly to A3/A4, the regime confound is negligible; if A2 performs markedly differently, interpret its effect as "selection + regime" jointly and rely on A3/A4 for the pure selection effect.
- Seeds: ≥3 seeds per arm where stochasticity exists (A4 explicitly seeded; decoding greedy/deterministic for generation tasks). Report seed-level variance; for deterministic arms, replicate over dataset subsamples.
- Order/position sanity check: verify block scores vary with query position across contexts in A1 (a positive control that selection is actually dynamic and non-degenerate before ablations).
- Calibration gate (from §2): key-scale matching verified on a held-out calibration slice; if B2/B4 entropy distributions are wildly different, re-tune normalization before main runs.

=====================================================================
4. ANALYSIS PLAN
=====================================================================
Metrics per suite:
- Long-context LM: per-token perplexity / NLL as a function of context length (bucketed, e.g., 4k–64k+), plus local vs. distant token NLL splits (distant-token NLL is the most sensitive to memory behavior; local should be nearly flat across arms — an internal sanity check).
- Needle-in-a-haystack: exact retrieval accuracy by depth × context-length grid.
- QA/summarization (LongBench/ZeroSCROLLS-style): task metric (F1/EM/ROUGE), with input-length stratification.

Statistical analysis:
- Two-way factorial ANOVA-style decomposition (or mixed-effects model with seed/dataset random effects) on each metric: main effect of A, main effect of B, A×B interaction, with bootstrap CIs (cluster bootstrap over documents).
- Effect sizes reported as absolute deltas vs. A1×B1 and as Cohen's d-style standardized effects; paired comparisons (same inputs across arms) to maximize power.
- Interaction interpretation: e.g., if B2 ≈ B1 under A1 but B2 ≪ B1 under A4/A3, representation quality matters only when selection is dynamic — the joint-contribution answer. If main effect of A is large and B effects are flat, lookup is critical and representation is redundant; if B4 (random keys) ≈ B1, the selection signal itself is not doing the work (suspicious — triggers a mechanism audit); if A3/A4 ≈ A1, "dynamic" lookup per se adds nothing beyond budget-matched static selection.
- Decision criteria (pre-registered thresholds, to be finalized once baseline variance is known): a component is "critical" if its ablation costs >10% relative on retrieval accuracy or >0.2 nats/token on distant-token NLL with CIs excluding zero, across ≥2 task suites; "redundant" if deltas are within noise (<2% / <0.05 nats); intermediate results reported as graded sensitivity rather than forced into binary labels. The A×B interaction is deemed meaningful only if its effect size exceeds the sum of marginal main-effect predictions with CI excluding zero.
- A5 sweep analyzed as monotonic sensitivity of performance to k; the k at which performance saturates indicates how much selection precision is needed.

=====================================================================
5. FEASIBILITY AND RISKS
=====================================================================
- Primary design is inference-only: justified because (per assumption A3) InfLLM is trained for short contexts and applied training-free to long ones, so ablations of the selection policy and key construction are implementable by modifying inference code, not weights. Cost: 16 core arms + 5 sweep runs + 2 controls ≈ 23 configurations; at 7B, 32k-token contexts, a few hundred to a few thousand examples per suite — nontrivial but tractable on a single A100-class GPU over days. If any ablation requires retraining (e.g., if the block reader is entangled with read-out in the actual implementation), cost grows by orders of magnitude; the trained-variant path (re-fitting adaptation parameters per arm on the assumed 8k training recipe) is listed as an extension, not the primary design.
- Scale assumptions: 7B primary. A small proxy (e.g., 1B-class model with the same mechanism re-implemented) may be used for smoke tests only (verifying arm implementations, calibration gates); it is explicitly NOT conclusion-supporting, because block-selection behavior may not transfer across scales.
- Benchmark availability offline: datasets (PG19/proof-pile subsets, NIAH generators, LongBench/ZeroSCROLLS) are not present in the sandbox and network is disabled; obtainability in the execution environment is unconfirmed and is a gating feasibility item.
- Compute/runtime budget is an unknown: no GPU here, no dependency environment; the numbers above are planning estimates, not verified runtimes.
- Main risks: (i) architecture assumptions wrong → arms redefined (factorial structure survives); (ii) OOD confound on A2 → mitigated by budget-matched A3/A4; (iii) key-scale nuisance in B → mitigated by normalization + entropy calibration gate; (iv) B4 floor control may be too degenerate (uniform selection) making it partially an A-arm — mitigated by seeding random keys with content-correlated noise (random projection retains some signal) and interpreting B4 as a floor, not a pure B level; (v) interaction effects may be small relative to seed/document variance → paired designs and clustering over documents.

6. SCOPE STATEMENT

This is a design-only deliverable. No experiment has been run, no data collected, and no results are claimed. The expected empirical outcome — which of dynamic lookup and unit representations is critical, redundant, or interacting — is unknown a priori; the design is built to distinguish these outcomes rather than anticipate them. Unverified \u2014 scale and base checkpoint are assumptions.\n(A2) Mechanism: context split into fixed-size memory blocks (block size assumed in the thousands of tokens; exact value unverified); per-block unit representation computed by a block reader using a representative token + learnable gating; query-conditioned top-k selection (k small, exact value unverified) over block keys; local sliding window always active.\n(A3) Training-free inference: block-selection machinery is learned on short sequences (~8k tokens, assumed) and applied zero-shot to long contexts; therefore factor manipulations are implementable at inference time without retraining.\n(A4) Tasks: long-context LM perplexity and retrieval/QA suites are the standard evaluation surface.\nAny mismatch between these assumptions and the actual implementation (e.g., learned top-k thresholds, different block-reader construction) requires arm redefinition but not redesign of the factorial structure.\n\n=====================================================================\n2. FULL ARM SPECIFICATION\n=====================================================================\nFactor A \u2014 dynamic memory lookup policy (4 levels):\n- A1 (reference): Full InfLLM. Query-conditioned top-k selection over block keys + local sliding window. Everything as assumed from the paper.\n- A2 (removal / dense): No dynamic lookup. Attention over ALL blocks uniformly \u2014 i.e., naive long-context attention restricted to the same block partition, same local window. This isolates the value of selective routing given the same stored memory.\n- A3 (static/position-based, budget-matched): Select the same number of blocks as A1 (top-k), but by position (blocks nearest the query) or by a fixed, query-independent pattern. Same compute and same number of attended blocks as A1 \u2014 this is the key OOD-confound control (see \u00a73).\n- A4 (random, budget-matched): Select k blocks uniformly at random per query token (fixed seed per example). Same budget as A1, selection signal destroyed.\n- A5 (budget sweep, optional secondary): top-k \u2208 {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} with A1's policy, to map the sensitivity curve of selection precision. Analyzed as a dose-response sub-study, not part of the 4\u00d74 core.\n\nFactor B \u2014 unit representation scheme (4 levels):\n- B1 (reference): Original block-reader unit representations (representative token + learnable gating), as assumed.\n- B2: Mean-pooled block encodings \u2014 mean over block token hidden states, projected to the key space.\n- B3: Single-token keys \u2014 the block's representative token's hidden state only, no gating.\n- B4 (floor control): Degenerate keys \u2014 frozen random projections of block content (or even fixed random vectors per block index), refreshed per seed. Establishes the selection-signal floor: performance when block keys carry no task-relevant signal.\n\nNuisance scale-matching (critical for clean B attribution): substituting keys changes their norm/scale, which after softmax temperature acts as an effective temperature change, not just a signal change. For B2\u2013B4, normalize replacement keys to match the L2 norm distribution of B1 keys (per-layer, per-head if applicable), and verify empirically that the top-k selection entropy distribution over blocks is comparable for B1 vs. B2 on a calibration subset before the main run. Additionally: value/pathway (what is actually attended to after selection) is held IDENTICAL across B arms \u2014 only the routing key changes \u2014 so B isolates the representation's role in routing, not in reading. (If the assumed block reader also affects the read-out pathway, add a B1-read/B2-route cross arm to decompose this; treat as a design contingency.)\n\nCore factorial: A1\u2013A4 \u00d7 B1\u2013B4 (16 arms) + A5 sweep (5 extra runs at B1, optionally one at B2). All arms share identical block partitioning, block size, local window size, KV storage, sampling/decoding settings.\n\n=====================================================================\n3. CONTROLS\n=====================================================================\n- Sliding-window-only baseline: local window active, memory machinery disabled entirely. Establishes what the memory adds at all.\n- Short-context reference: base model (or InfLLM within its trained context length, assumed 8k) evaluated on truncated versions of the same inputs \u2014 separates \"long-context ability\" from \"short-context competence.\"\n- Fixed geometry: block size, number of stored blocks, local window, and total attention budget held constant across all arms so effects are attributable to policy/representation, not to compute or coverage.\n- OOD-regime confound control: A2 (uniform attention over all blocks) both removes selection AND changes the attention distribution regime. A3 and A4 keep the regime (same sparse top-k structure, same budget) and change only the selection signal; the contrast A1 \u2212 A3/A4 measures the value of *informed* selection, while A1 \u2212 A2 additionally includes any regime shift. If A2 performs similarly to A3/A4, the regime confound is negligible; if A2 performs markedly differently, interpret its effect as \"selection + regime\" jointly and rely on A3/A4 for the pure selection effect.\n- Seeds: \u22653 seeds per arm where stochasticity exists (A4 explicitly seeded; decoding greedy/deterministic for generation tasks). Report seed-level variance; for deterministic arms, replicate over dataset subsamples.\n- Order/position sanity check: verify block scores vary with query position across contexts in A1 (a positive control that selection is actually dynamic and non-degenerate before ablations).\n- Calibration gate (from \u00a72): key-scale matching verified on a held-out calibration slice; if B2/B4 entropy distributions are wildly different, re-tune normalization before main runs.\n\n=====================================================================\n4. ANALYSIS PLAN\n=====================================================================\nMetrics per suite:\n- Long-context LM: per-token perplexity / NLL as a function of context length (bucketed, e.g., 4k\u201364k+), plus local vs. distant token NLL splits (distant-token NLL is the most sensitive to memory behavior; local should be nearly flat across arms \u2014 an internal sanity check).\n- Needle-in-a-haystack: exact retrieval accuracy by depth \u00d7 context-length grid.\n- QA/summarization (LongBench/ZeroSCROLLS-style): task metric (F1/EM/ROUGE), with input-length stratification.\n\nStatistical analysis:\n- Two-way factorial ANOVA-style decomposition (or mixed-effects model with seed/dataset random effects) on each metric: main effect of A, main effect of B, A\u00d7B interaction, with bootstrap CIs (cluster bootstrap over documents).\n- Effect sizes reported as absolute deltas vs. A1\u00d7B1 and as Cohen's d-style standardized effects; paired comparisons (same inputs across arms) to maximize power.\n- Interaction interpretation: e.g., if B2 \u2248 B1 under A1 but B2 \u226a B1 under A4/A3, representation quality matters only when selection is dynamic \u2014 the joint-contribution answer. If main effect of A is large and B effects are flat, lookup is critical and representation is redundant; if B4 (random keys) \u2248 B1, the selection signal itself is not doing the work (suspicious \u2014 triggers a mechanism audit); if A3/A4 \u2248 A1, \"dynamic\" lookup per se adds nothing beyond budget-matched static selection.\n- Decision criteria (pre-registered thresholds, to be finalized once baseline variance is known): a component is \"critical\" if its ablation costs >10% relative on retrieval accuracy or >0.2 nats/token on distant-token NLL with CIs excluding zero, across \u22652 task suites; \"redundant\" if deltas are within noise (<2% / <0.05 nats); intermediate results reported as graded sensitivity rather than forced into binary labels. The A\u00d7B interaction is deemed meaningful only if its effect size exceeds the sum of marginal main-effect predictions with CI excluding zero.\n- A5 sweep analyzed as monotonic sensitivity of performance to k; the k at which performance saturates indicates how much selection precision is needed.\n\n=====================================================================\n5. FEASIBILITY AND RISKS\n=====================================================================\n- Primary design is inference-only: justified because (per assumption A3) InfLLM is trained for short contexts and applied training-free to long ones, so ablations of the selection policy and key construction are implementable by modifying inference code, not weights. Cost: 16 core arms + 5 sweep runs + 2 controls \u2248 23 configurations; at 7B, 32k-token contexts, a few hundred to a few thousand examples per suite \u2014 nontrivial but tractable on a single A100-class GPU over days. If any ablation requires retraining (e.g., if the block reader is entangled with read-out in the actual implementation), cost grows by orders of magnitude; the trained-variant path (re-fitting adaptation parameters per arm on the assumed 8k training recipe) is listed as an extension, not the primary design.\n- Scale assumptions: 7B primary. A small proxy (e.g., 1B-class model with the same mechanism re-implemented) may be used for smoke tests only (verifying arm implementations, calibration gates); it is explicitly NOT conclusion-supporting, because block-selection behavior may not transfer across scales.\n- Benchmark availability offline: datasets (PG19/proof-pile subsets, NIAH generators, LongBench/ZeroSCROLLS) are not present in the sandbox and network is disabled; obtainability in the execution environment is unconfirmed and is a gating feasibility item.\n- Compute/runtime budget is an unknown: no GPU here, no dependency environment; the numbers above are planning estimates, not verified runtimes.\n- Main risks: (i) architecture assumptions wrong \u2192 arms redefined (factorial structure survives); (ii) OOD confound on A2 \u2192 mitigated by budget-matched A3/A4; (iii) key-scale nuisance in B \u2192 mitigated by normalization + entropy calibration gate; (iv) B4 floor control may be too degenerate (uniform selection) making it partially an A-arm \u2014 mitigated by seeding random keys with content-correlated noise (random projection retains some signal) and interpreting B4 as a floor, not a pure B level; (v) interaction effects may be small relative to seed/document variance \u2192 paired designs and clustering over documents.\n\n=====================================================================\n6.
